answer-para2.content: Batching requests improves GPU utilisation during LLM inference primarily because GPUs are massively parallel processors that waste enormous amounts of compute when they run with low occupancy. When you serve a single request at a time, the GPU's thousands of cores are largely idle, since a lone small matrix multiplication cannot fill the hardware's parallel execution units, leaving much of the silicon doing nothing while waiting for memory operations. By grouping multiple requests together into a batch, you create larger tensor operations that keep many cores busy simultaneously, dramatically increasing the fraction of the GPU's theoretical peak performance that is actually being used. This matters especially during the prefill phase, where processing many tokens at once is highly parallelisable, but it also helps during decoding by reducing the relative overhead of kernel launches and memory transfers. Without batching, you pay the fixed costs of launching GPU kernels and moving data between memory and compute for each request individually, so throughput collapses and latency per request suffers. Batching amortises these fixed costs across many requests, allowing the expensive memory bandwidth and compute resources to be shared efficiently, which is why production inference servers like vLLM and TensorRT-LLM rely heavily on dynamic and continuous batching to maximise throughput and keep the hardware working at high utilisation.
